newsitem.title: EL SALVADOR: Left, right appear even in El Salvador vote.
newsitem.headline: Left, right appear even in El Salvador vote.

text.p: Former leftist guerrillas claimed on Tuesday to have tied with the right-wing ruling party in mid-term elections for Congress, and a U.S. official praised democratic advances in this war-torn nation.

Based on partial results from Sunday's voting, the Farabundo Marti National Liberation Front (FMLN) said it had gained a 28-28 tie with the Republican National Alliance (ARENA) in the 84-seat Congress. ARENA holds a 39-21 edge over the opposition FMLN in the current Congress.
With 58 percent of the votes counted, the FMLN also claimed it would take more than 50 of the country's 262 town halls, including the capital city of San Salvador.
ARENA was seen winning more than 100 towns with others going to 11 smaller parties.
The Supreme Electoral Tribunal said it stopped counting ballots on Monday night because of "technical failures" and that a final count could be days away.
Although ARENA still holds the upper hand, the ruling party suffered the first serious dent in its electoral armor since coming to power in 1989.
The vote was the first show of strength for the FMLN since signing a peace treaty in 1992 that ended a bloody civil war and a major advance over its drubbing in the 1994 election.

"If the FMLN did well, so be it. It's a democratic process where everybody gets a chance to run and get elected," U.S. Assistant Secretary of State for Inter-American Affairs Jeffrey Davidow said late on Monday during a visit to Panama.

In the 1980s, the United States poured billions of dollars into El Salvador to prevent a military victory by the FMLN, but U.S. involvement dwindled significatnly after the previous ARENA government signed a 1992 peace treaty with the rebels.
Business and political leaders on Tuesday called attention to the stunning FMLN gains and called for changes by ARENA.

"I think the party has to open up, modernize internally, it has to increase participation and show a little humility," Luis Cardenal, president of the Chamber of Commerce and Industry, told reporters.
President Armando Calderon said on Monday the vote meant his party must redouble efforts to create jobs and fight crime.

Ruben Zamora, president of the center-left Social Christian Party, said ARENA was hurt by its poor performance in government and Congress, adding that aggressive campaign techniques didn't help either.
"They played with fire and they got burned," Zamora said of the ARENA campaign, which recalled guerrilla violence during the 12-year civil war that left 75,000 dead.
Many Salvadoran voters, however, were only reminded of the government's vicious counterinsurgency campaign and appalling human rights record, Zamora said.
